extracted.intended_audience: public_relations professionals and press-release writers (and media researchers interested in PR-news relations)
extracted.subtask_description: Empirically derived criteria predicting whether a press release (or PR-origin material) will be picked up and run by newspapers and newswires; useful for PR practitioners aiming to maximize media pickup. Based on content-analysis of UK national newspapers and broadcast items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire-friendliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release reach the wire (PA / AP) and is it formatted so the wire desk will run it largely intact? Wire pickup is the strongest single predictor of newspaper printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format releases for wire consumption: concise lead, clear attributions, no promotional language or extraneous material that the wire will strip. Consider distribution channels—getting the release onto the PA/AP wire greatly increases chance of newspaper pickup. Scoring note: high if release is sent to/compatible with wire desks and appears publishable without heavy rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the release pegged to a beat with high known PR uptake (health, business, entertainment) and framed to that beat's editorial conventions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor angle, tone, and evidence to the conventions and information needs of the target desk. Health, business and entertainment desks accept PR copy at much higher rates; politics and crime show lower uptake. Scoring: higher when beat fit is explicit and matches beats with historically high PR dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR-origin laundering tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release read as if a journalist could have written it (allowing newspapers to run PR-sourced material without overt attribution to PR origin)? Releases that obscure promotional origin are more pickup-worthy than overtly promotional copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overtly promotional phrasing, marketing calls-to-action, or obvious PR framing that flags the item as 'advertorial.' Use neutral reporting style and include facts/quotes that look like journalist-sourced material. Anti-pattern: highly promotional, salesy language that makes editors reject or rework the item heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-source sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release supply enough quotes, statistics, and context that a reporter can file from the release alone? When a release supplies sufficient material, pickup is far higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark: could a sub-editor or reporter publish from the release within ~15 minutes? Include ready-to-use quotes, clear facts/statistics, and brief contextual framing so minimal additional reporting is needed. Scoring: high if the release can stand alone as a publishable story with minimal verification/research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-association rewriting tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are releases optimized for the wire's rewrite step (clean leads, clear attribution, no hyperlinks, no embedded HTML) so they survive PA/AP transformation more intact?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove HTML, embedded links, and nonstandard formatting; write clean inverted-pyramid leads and standard attributions. The more the text conforms to wire-desk expectations, the less it will be altered and the more likely it will be reprinted verbatim. Example checklist: plain text, dateline/lead clarity, attribution in journalist-style, no embedded multimedia code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-week news-cycle calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the release pegged to ongoing news themes within the current news cycle? Releases tied to ongoing debates or timely themes during the sampled weeks had higher pickup than orphan announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link announcements to current policy debates, trending topics, or known editorial agendas where possible. Timeliness and thematic relevance within the immediate news window raise pickup probability. Anti-pattern: isolated announcements with no link to current coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the source have institutional rank (government departments, large corporations, major universities)? Institutional sources had disproportionately high uptake; small NGOs and grassroots groups had near-zero pickup despite comparable newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage recognizable institutional credibility where possible (partnerships, endorsements, reputable spokespeople) to increase pickup. Be aware of subsidy-asymmetry: editors favor authoritative institutional sources. Scoring: higher for releases from high-status organizations or with prominent institutional backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction-to-headline test
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story have a clean single-sentence summary in the lead that can be reduced to a headline? Stories with a clear single-sentence lead were converted to wire copy more reliably than discursive releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a tight, headline-friendly lead: one sentence that encapsulates the news hook. If the lead can be turned directly into a headline, the release is more wire-friendly and more likely to be printed. Scoring: high if lead yields an obvious headline and succinct news peg.
